body.text: Myanmar’s military authorities have imported Iranian jet fuel using “sham paperwork” designed to circumvent the U.S. sanctions on both nations, according to reports published by Reuters and a local activist group yesterday.

The reports, which were based on shipping records, satellite imagery, and documents from Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator and Ministry of Commerce, show how both the origin and content of the shipments were falsified. These shipments of jet fuel, which were disguised as diesel, have allowed the Myanmar Air Force to sustain its brutal air campaign against those opposing its coup d’etat in February 2021.

It has been clear for some time that Myanmar’s military was receiving fuel shipments from Iran’s large tanker “shadow fleet” – both Reuters and the rights group Amnesty International have reported on the issue – but the exact mechanism by which the shipments were being concealed was previously unknown.

The Reuters report traced the journey of a particular vessel, the U.S.-sanctioned tanker Reef, which arrived in Myanmar waters in December of last year with some 113,000 barrels of fuel aboard. As the report detailed, the shipment was ordered by Myanmar-based energy broker Dynamic Wave, which signed a $15.8 million sales contract with Thailand’s Tawan-Oil Trading “to supposedly take delivery of a similar amount of South African diesel.”

But the vessel really contained jet fuel from Iran, which Reuters verified both via documentary evidence and satellite images and analysis provided by SynMax Intelligence, “which tracked the tanker’s journey from the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas to Southeast Asia.”

Myanmar’s military junta, which in April pupated into a quasi-civilian government under coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, was involved in concealing the origin and nature of the shipment. Days before the Reef arrived, Reuters stated, Myanmar’s foreign exchange regulator told the client of Dynamic Wave that it would issue import documentation that labeled the delivery as diesel “instead of jet fuel,” according to a copy of a November 30 letter seen by the news agency.

Reuters said that it received the document from the local activist group Justice for Myanmar (JFM), which also published a report yesterday providing more detailed evidence of how Myanmar and Iran had concealed the shipments. In its report, JFM stated that leaked import documentation “reveals a network of junta-linked businesses in Myanmar, Thailand, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), for fuel declared as originating in or transiting through Singapore and South Africa.”

Between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said that it identified records from the Myanmar Commerce Ministry for six shipments of jet fuel that included more than 843,000 barrels of aviation fuel, valued at $109.5 million. Earlier this month, Reuters reported that shipments of jet fuel between Iran and Myanmar have continued into 2026, stating that a tanker reached Myanmar in September.

According to previous reports, Iranian “shadow tankers” have also used a number of other methods to conceal their shipments. They have “gone dark” and switched off their location signals when onloading or offloading aviation fuel. Fuel shipments have also been resold and transshipped multiple times in order to hide the source.

All of this demonstrates the lengths to which Myanmar’s military is prepared to go to ensure a continued supply of jet fuel, as well as the porous nature of U.S. sanctions against both Iran and Myanmar.

In March 2023, the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions on two individuals and six entities linked to Myanmar’s jet-fuel industry, citing its deadly bombing campaign against civilian targets. In a statement at the time, Treasury said that the U.S. government “remains steadfast in its commitment to the people of Burma, and will continue to deny the military the materiel it uses to commit these atrocities.” Similar sanctions have also been imposed by the United Kingdom, European Union, Canada, and Australia.

These shipments from Iran have allowed the military to sustain its fierce air campaign against resistance groups and civilian populations that are believed to harbor them. As it has lost territory in various parts of the country, the Myanmar military has relied ever more heavily on its air force, one of its main advantages over the welter of rebel groups and civilian militias that oppose it.

According to the U.N. Human Rights Office, civilian deaths from airstrikes rose by more than 50 percent in 2025. The figure increased from 641 in 2024 to 982 last year. The latter figure included 232 children, which, as JFM noted, is more children than were killed by airstrikes in the previous four years combined.

The past several months have been marked by fierce bombing attacks in Rakhine State, where the military is battling to retake territory from the Arakan Army (AA), a Rakhine nationalist group that has conquered most of the state since late 2023. Airstrikes on two camps for internally displaced people in AA-controlled Ponnagyun township earlier this month killed at least eight people. These came after a major aerial attack in neighboring Kyauktaw township on September 28, which killed 50 people and wounded at least 58, according to the AA and other local sources.

Given its importance to the military’s machine of repression, human rights activists have campaigned since the coup for foreign governments to cut off its supplies of jet fuel. However, the fact that fuel continues to flow between Iran and Myanmar, despite extensive sanctions, demonstrates how difficult it can be for the United States and its partners to establish firm control over complex and attenuated global fuel supply chains.

JFM yesterday concluded its report by urging like-minded governments to close the gaps that have permitted the Myanmar military access to jet fuel. It called on the Thai, Singaporean, and Emirati authorities “to urgently investigate the junta’s trade fraud and use of companies in their territory to source aviation fuel.” It also said that the U.S. and other Western powers should “sanction the junta’s whole aviation fuel supply chain network, including the companies and individuals identified in this investigation.”
